newsitem.title: UK: UK gilts this week - haunted by politics, data.
newsitem.headline: UK gilts this week - haunted by politics, data.

text.p: UK government bonds (gilts) face a gruelling week, with a slew of key economic data and the start of the campaign for the May 1 general election.
"The final firing of the starting pistol will focus minds wonderfully although the market has been talking about the election for some time," said BZW analyst Kevin Adams.

Prime Minister John Major announced the election date on Monday, ending months of speculation. Gilts indulged in a knee-jerk wobble but analysts say the market has already largely discounted a change of government.
Adams said the market had built in a significant risk premium and was on a strong technical footing.
The UK's main opposition Labour party is expected to win the election, terminating 18 years of Conservative rule.
"People don't like uncertainty and that's what election announcements always mean," HSBC economist Don Smith. "On balance, I think gilts will end the week lower."

Labour has been traditionally regarded as the enemy of the gilt market, which would have to foot the bill for any expensive spending pledges but the promises of new Labour leader Tony Blair have wiped away most of the market's worries.
The party now says it will stick to the current Conservative government's public spending plans for the next two years and will also adhere to its inflation target of 2.5 percent or lower.
The Conservatives feel the economy will be their strong suit in the election campaign and this week's data should go their way, analysts say.
Wednesday's unemployment figures should show claimant unemployment falling by another 39,000, taking the unemployment rate down to 4.2 percent from 4.3 percent.
Government borrowing data due for release on Tuesday should show the government is on course to undershoot its forecast deficit of 26.5 billion stg for fiscal 1996-97 (April-March.)
Analysts are looking for a February deficit of 3.7 billion, taking the shortfall to around 14 billion for the first 11 months.

But the biggest data focus for the week is likely to be the retail sales release which is due on Wednesday. Analysts are looking for a February rise of just 0.1 percent, after a 0.6 percent bounce in January.

Weaker growth will support Chancellor of the Exchequer's contention that there is no need to raise Britain's 6.0 percent interest rates to contain demand but dealers warn than another strong figure will cause concern.
Retail price figures for February are due on Thursday and are likely to show the underlying rate slowing to an annual 2.9 percent from 3.1 percent in January.
Analysts say that the strength of sterling means the rate should be close to the official target by the summer.
